activities.title: Commitment & Ambivalence
activities.summary: Reflect on decision space and support needs without scoring whether you should stay or leave.
activities.intro: Think about the past month, or the nearest relevant period. These original prompts are educational, not a validated measure or diagnosis; scores cannot tell you what to do. Skip any item; a skipped answer means no overall band or recommendations. Cutoffs are illustrative, not clinical. Your result is stored on this device; consider whether using it is safe if someone else has access. If fear, coercion or violence is present, skip joint work and seek individual specialist support.

subscales.label: Clarity about my needs
subscales.description: How hard it feels to name your own needs and limits.

subscales.label: Room to decide
subscales.description: Whether pressure makes it difficult to consider choices.

subscales.label: Understanding options
subscales.description: Whether practical questions make possible paths hard to evaluate.

subscales.label: Support and reflection
subscales.description: Whether you have space and support to reflect independently.

bands.label: Some space for reflection
bands.narrative: Your responses suggest fewer reported barriers among the items answered. The score does not indicate whether to stay or separate, or whether a situation is safe.

bands.label: More space or information may help
bands.narrative: Your responses suggest uncertainty or pressure in some areas. You can seek independent information, take time, or choose a next step without sharing a decision.

bands.label: Consider individual support

If there is fear, coercion or violence, seek domestic abuse specialist support individually, not couples work.

activities.title: When partners want different things
activities.summary: Make space for uncertainty and different levels of readiness without labeling either person.

cards.heading: Different positions can coexist
cards.body: One person may want to work on the relationship while another is unsure, considering separation, or not ready to name a position. Either person can change their mind, and no position is a moral failure.

cards.heading: Uncertainty is not a vote
cards.body: A person does not owe an immediate decision, a complete explanation, or a promise to stay. The other person can also set limits on how long they are willing to remain in uncertainty. Neither can dictate the other’s choice.

cards.heading: Make space without extracting answers
cards.body: If both can speak freely and want to talk, ask “Would you like to share anything about where you are?” Accept “not now” as a complete answer. Do not ask for private writings or assessment results.

cards.heading: Support does not require agreement
cards.body: Each person may seek individual counseling or other trusted support without a shared decision. If fear, coercion or violence is present, do not use joint discernment; contact an individual domestic abuse specialist if safe.

takeaway.question: What is a respectful response to “I am not ready to say”?
options: Demand a deadline and private journal entries.
Accept the answer and consider your own needs independently.
Treat uncertainty as a promise to stay.
takeaway.explanation: A person may decide what to share and when; the other can also consider their own boundaries.

activities.title: Possible paths forward
activities.summary: Consider staying, separating, a limited effort, or taking time without implying one is best.

cards.heading: More than one next step
cards.body: Possible paths include continuing the current arrangement, taking time to gather information, trying a limited change while staying, or exploring separation. These are options, not a required sequence or exhaustive list.

cards.heading: Consider costs and needs
cards.body: For each option, notice what might improve, what could remain difficult, and what practical questions arise around housing, care, work or support. You do not need to solve these questions in the app or disclose private plans.

cards.heading: A decision belongs to each person
cards.body: A relationship effort requires ongoing voluntary participation; a person may choose not to continue it. Separation does not require the other person’s agreement to your internal decision. Avoid treating either outcome as failure.

cards.heading: Get information safely
cards.body: For personal legal, financial, housing or parenting questions, consult an appropriate independent local professional or support service. If leaving or discussing a change could increase danger, seek individual domestic abuse specialist support using a safer device.

takeaway.question: What can this module determine about the right path?
options: A score can determine whether you should separate.
It cannot decide; you may explore options and seek independent information.
Everyone should try the same six-month program first.
takeaway.explanation: Only you can make your own decisions; choices and timing depend on your circumstances and safety.

activities.title: Looking at my actions without taking blame
activities.summary: Reflect on choices you control without assuming equal responsibility for harm.

cards.heading: Use a concrete example
cards.body: For a non-abusive disagreement, identify something you said or did and its effect: “I interrupted when we were discussing plans.” Consider what you might do differently without making a claim about the other person’s motives.

cards.heading: Responsibility has limits
cards.body: You are responsible for your choices, not another person’s threats, abuse, control, or violence. Trying to avoid someone’s anger does not cause their abusive behavior. Shared patterns must not obscure unequal power or responsibility.

cards.heading: Avoid forced confession
cards.body: This reflection is not a demand to list faults or hand an inventory to a partner. You may skip a topic, use an abstract example, or seek individual help rather than write it down.

cards.heading: Choose an action for yourself
cards.body: A possible action might be to seek support, set a limit, or communicate differently where safe. It does not require agreeing to reconciliation, accepting mistreatment, or staying in a conversation.

takeaway.question: How should personal reflection treat abuse?
options: Both people are equally responsible for one person’s abuse.
The person using abuse is responsible; the other person is not required to fix it.
A person must share a list of faults to prove good faith.
takeaway.explanation: Accountability is specific to each person’s actions and must not blame someone for abuse.

activities.title: A time-limited effort, if freely chosen
activities.summary: Define an optional relationship effort without making six months or any outcome mandatory.

cards.heading: A trial is one option
cards.body: Some people choose to try specific changes for a period; others choose separation, maintain their current arrangement, or need more time. A trial is not a prerequisite for leaving and should not be proposed where coercion or violence is present.

cards.heading: Make consent ongoing
cards.body: If both freely want a trial, discuss what each is willing to do and for how long. Either person may decline, change their mind, or stop. A deadline is for review, not a promise to stay or reconcile.

cards.heading: Use observable, bounded actions
cards.body: Rather than “try harder,” identify an action such as one optional 15-minute planning check each week, the person responsible, and what happens if it is missed. Include individual rest, support, and limits; do not demand passwords or private writing.

cards.heading: Review without a verdict
cards.body: At the chosen review, each person can ask whether actions occurred, how they felt, and what they want next. Continuing, changing the plan, taking time, or separating can all remain possibilities. Seek independent professional support as useful.

takeaway.question: What makes an optional trial respectful?
options: A fixed six-month promise that cannot be withdrawn.
Specific actions and a review point, with consent that can be withdrawn.
Mandatory sharing of all private thoughts.
takeaway.explanation: A review is not a commitment to a particular outcome, and consent can be withdrawn.

bands.narrative: Your conflicts are fairly contained. This module can still give you tools for the moments that do heat up, and a shared language for them.

activities.title: Your body in a fight
activities.summary: Why you can't think straight mid-argument, and what that means for how you fight.

cards.heading: The alarm goes off
cards.body: When an argument feels threatening, your body reacts as if you were in danger. Your heart speeds up, stress hormones surge, and blood moves toward your muscles and away from the parts of the brain that handle nuance, empathy and memory.

cards.heading: This is called flooding
cards.body: Once you're flooded, you can't really listen. You hear criticism that wasn't intended, forget what your partner said a minute ago, and reach for whatever will end the threat: attack, defend or escape. Neither of you is choosing to be like this. It's biology.

cards.heading: Know your signals
cards.body: Common signs: a racing heart (many people notice it climbing past about 100 beats per minute), a hot face, clenched jaw or fists, tunnel vision, a blank mind, or a strong urge to leave. Everyone's signals are different, so it helps to know your own.

cards.heading: What helps
cards.body: You can't reason your way out of flooding. You have to calm your body first. That usually takes at least 20 minutes of real rest, without rehearsing the argument in your head. After that, you can come back and actually talk.

takeaway.question: Your partner is flooded mid-argument. What's most likely to help?
options: Explain your point more clearly so they understand
Pause for at least 20 minutes and calm down separately
Keep going until you reach a resolution
takeaway.explanation: A flooded brain can't take in new information. Pausing isn't giving up. It gives you both your thinking brains back.

sources: Gottman, J. M. & Silver, N. (1999). The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work. (Concept: physiological flooding.)

activities.title: It's you two against the cycle
activities.summary: The real enemy isn't your partner. It's the pattern you both get caught in.

cards.heading: Fights have a shape
cards.body: If you look closely, most of your fights follow the same steps, even when the topic changes. One of you reaches, pushes or protests, and the other pulls back, defends or goes quiet. Each move triggers the next.

cards.heading: A common pattern
cards.body: A very common version: one partner pursues (they criticize, push for answers, raise their voice) because they feel alone. The other withdraws (they go quiet, leave, minimize) because they feel they're failing. The more one pursues, the more the other withdraws, and the reverse is also true.

cards.heading: Both moves make sense
cards.body: Under the pursuing there is usually fear of being unimportant or abandoned. Under the withdrawing there is usually fear of failing, being judged, or making things worse. Both partners are trying to protect the relationship in the only way they know in that moment.

cards.heading: Name the cycle, not the person
cards.body: When you can say "we're in the cycle again" instead of "you always…", you stop being opponents. You become two people facing a shared problem, and that is where change starts.

takeaway.question: Which statement names the cycle rather than blaming a person?
options: You always shut down when I need you.
I think the pattern grabbed us again. I'm pushing and you're pulling away.
If you would just listen, we wouldn't fight.

sources: Johnson, S. (2008). Hold Me Tight. (Concept: the negative interaction cycle, Emotionally Focused Therapy.)

activities.title: Why winning loses
activities.summary: In a relationship, if one of you wins the argument, you both lose something.

cards.heading: The scoreboard trap
cards.body: In a heated moment, being right feels urgent. You bring up evidence, remember past offenses, and correct the details. Even when you "win", your partner walks away feeling smaller, and the distance between you grows.

cards.heading: What you actually want
cards.body: Ask yourself: "Do I want to be right, or do I want to be close?" Usually what you want is to be understood, to feel safe, and to know you matter. None of those comes from defeating your partner.

cards.heading: Escalation is a warning sign
cards.body: Insults, contempt, threats and bringing up a whole history of grievances cause lasting damage. If fights regularly include these, or anyone feels afraid, that is more than a communication problem. Safety comes first. See Safety & Support in your profile.

cards.heading: A different goal
cards.body: Change the goal of a disagreement from "settle who's right" to "both of us understand each other a little better". It's a smaller target, but you can actually hit it.

takeaway.question: In your next disagreement, what will you aim for?
options: Ending calmly, even without a solution
takeaway.explanation: There's no wrong answer. Pick one and notice what changes.

activities.title: Taking a break the right way
activities.summary: How to pause a fight without it feeling like abandonment.

cards.heading: Not all breaks are equal
cards.body: Walking out mid-sentence, slamming a door, or going silent for two days are all breaks, and they usually make things worse. To a partner who tends to pursue, they feel like abandonment.

cards.heading: The four parts of a good break
cards.body:
1. Use the signal you agreed on ahead of time.
2. Say when you'll come back ("I need 30 minutes. I'll find you at 8.").
3. Spend the time actually calming down: walk, breathe, listen to music. Don't rehearse your arguments.
4. Come back when you said you would, even if only to set a new time.

cards.heading: Coming back is the repair
cards.body: The promise to return is what makes a break feel safe. Every time you come back when you said you would, your partner learns that a pause doesn't mean you're leaving.

cards.heading: Either partner can call it
cards.body: A break isn't a punishment or a way to avoid the topic. Anyone who notices flooding, in themselves or in the other person, can call one, and the other partner agrees to honor it.

takeaway.question: Which part of a break most helps your partner trust it?
options: Leaving quickly before things get worse
Saying when you'll come back, and doing it
Explaining why they upset you before you go

activities.title: A ceasefire is not avoidance
activities.summary: Why setting hot topics aside for a short time can be the bravest next step.

cards.heading: You can't repair a house that's on fire
cards.body: When fighting is constant, every attempt to "finally deal with it" adds fuel. A short, agreed pause on the hottest topics gives both of you room to breathe and to remember that you're on the same side.

cards.heading: What a ceasefire is
cards.body: It is time-limited (usually 1–2 weeks), agreed by both of you, and comes with a list of the topics you are setting aside, not erasing. Those topics go in the "parking lot" and you will come back to them, with better tools.

cards.heading: What a ceasefire is not
cards.body: It isn't pretending everything is fine, and it isn't one partner silencing the other. It must never be used to hide anything unsafe. Safety concerns always come first.

cards.heading: Use the space well
cards.body: During the ceasefire, put energy into small moments of connection: a daily appreciation, a short walk, a shared meal. They rebuild the goodwill that hard conversations depend on.

takeaway.question: What makes a ceasefire different from avoidance?
options: It's agreed by both partners and has an end date
One partner decides the other shouldn't bring things up
The topics are dropped for good

activities.summary: Trace the steps of your typical fight so you can recognize it as it starts.
activities.intro: Think of a recent argument that followed a familiar pattern. You'll map what you did, what you felt underneath, and what you think your partner did. Do it alone first. You can share it later in "Naming our cycle together".

steps.prompt: What usually sets it off? Describe the moment the temperature starts rising.

steps.prompt: What do I see my partner do in response?

activities.title: My flooding signals

steps.prompt: What do I notice in my body?

activities.title: My self-soothing toolkit
activities.summary: Build a personal list of what actually calms you down, and practice one now.
activities.intro: During a break, what you do matters. Rehearsing the argument keeps you flooded. Real soothing brings your body back down.

steps.prompt: What tends to calm me?
Anything else that works for me?
What makes me MORE wound up, even if it's tempting? (for example, texting friends about the fight, or scrolling)
Let's practice. Breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, and breathe out slowly for 6. Making the exhale longer than the inhale signals your body that it's safe.
Breathe slowly for two minutes.

activities.outro: Your toolkit is saved. You'll find it any time you start a time-out.

activities.title: Our time-out agreement
activities.summary: Draft the rules for pausing a fight, then confirm them together.

steps.prompt: What's our signal? (a word, a phrase, a hand gesture, for example "timeout" or "I'm getting flooded")

activities.title: Communication Patterns
activities.summary: Reflect on requests, defensiveness, respect, withdrawal, and listening.
activities.intro: Think about the past month. This original, unvalidated reflection is not a diagnosis or a safety screen; scores show patterns to explore, not who is right. Answer from your own perspective. Skip this activity if it feels unsafe. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, seek individual safety and specialized support instead of couples activities.

subscales.label: Specific requests are hard
subscales.description: Global judgments versus specific requests.

subscales.label: Defensive responses
subscales.description: Difficulty hearing feedback without counterattacking.

subscales.label: Disrespectful language
subscales.description: Mockery or dismissive reactions when upset.

subscales.label: Unexplained withdrawal

subscales.label: Being understood

items.text: I describe my partner as the problem instead of naming a specific action.
When I raise a concern, I ask for a specific change.
When I hear a complaint, I respond with a counter-complaint.
I can acknowledge a part of a concern without accepting blame for everything.
Sarcasm, eye-rolling, or mockery enters our disagreements.
Even when frustrated, I speak without insulting my partner.
A discussion ends in silence without anyone explaining whether they want to return to it.
When I need a break, I can say so without using it as punishment.
I feel interrupted before I can finish a thought.
Someone checks whether they understood me before responding.

bands.label: Fewer concerns noticed
bands.narrative: Your answers suggest fewer difficulties in these particular areas. A low score does not establish safety or invalidate a specific hurt. Choose a skill you want to practice.

bands.label: Some concerns noticed
bands.narrative: A few patterns may deserve attention. Review the higher-concern areas, then try one specific change on a low-stakes topic if you both want to.

bands.label: More concerns noticed
bands.narrative: Communication may feel difficult in several areas. Consider individual or relationship support as appropriate; if fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support, not couples activities.

activities.title: Complaints vs. criticism
activities.summary: Name an observable action without turning it into a verdict about someone.

cards.heading: A complaint has an address
cards.body: A complaint points to something specific that happened and its effect: “The dishes were still in the sink this morning, and I felt rushed.” Criticism turns a moment into a character judgment: “You are lazy.”

cards.heading: Replace the verdict
cards.body: Pick one recent, observable event; leave out “always,” “never,” and motives you cannot know. Describe its impact on you without presenting your interpretation as a fact.

cards.heading: Make a request, not a demand
cards.body: Try: “Could we decide who washes the dishes tonight?” A request can be answered with no or a different proposal. If the answer is no, you can decide what boundary or practical step you need.

cards.heading: Respect does not excuse harm
cards.body: Softer wording is a tool, not a requirement to earn respectful treatment. You are not responsible for another person’s intimidation or violence. Stop and seek individual support if raising concerns feels unsafe.

takeaway.question: Which opening is a specific complaint rather than a character attack?
options: “When the dishes were left, I felt rushed; could we make a plan?”
takeaway.explanation: The second identifies an event, an impact, and a request without labeling the person.

activities.title: The gentle start-up
activities.summary: Use a feeling, a situation, and a doable request without suppressing a boundary.

cards.heading: Start with one moment
cards.body: Choose a calm time and ask whether the other person is willing to talk. “Is now okay to talk for ten minutes about the grocery plan?” If either says no, you can stop.

cards.heading: Name situation, feeling, and need
cards.body: Try: “When our plan for groceries changed without a message, I felt stressed because I need notice. Could you text me if the plan changes?” Avoid assuming intent or requiring a particular response.

cards.heading: Check that the request can be answered
cards.body: Make it specific about action and timing. “Text before 5 if you cannot shop” is clearer than “be more considerate.” Ask what would be workable for the other person.

cards.heading: If the response is not respectful
cards.body: A gentle start cannot control another person’s behavior. End the exchange if it becomes insulting or frightening. You may keep your boundary regardless of whether the other person agrees.

takeaway.question: What makes a request easier to answer?
options: It names a specific action and time.
It proves your partner meant harm.
It leaves no room for disagreement.
takeaway.explanation: A clear request makes possible responses visible; it is not a demand.

activities.title: Listening to understand
activities.summary: Practice checking the message before preparing your response.

cards.heading: Listen for the point, not the rebuttal
cards.body: Put aside your counterexample for one short turn. Notice the event, the feeling the speaker names, and the request, if any. You can take a break rather than force attention.

cards.heading: Reflect tentatively
cards.body: Say “What I heard was that the late change left you stressed. Did I get that?” Let the speaker correct you; the listener does not need to repeat every word.

cards.heading: Clarify before defending
cards.body: Ask one focused question such as “Was the hard part the change itself, or not knowing?” Do not cross-examine or demand examples the speaker does not want to give.

cards.heading: Then take your turn
cards.body: Once the speaker says the summary is close enough, ask if they have capacity to hear your view. Understanding is not agreement, and each person can decline or stop.

takeaway.question: What is a useful first response after listening?
options: “What I heard was… did I get it?”
takeaway.explanation: A tentative summary gives the speaker room to correct you.

activities.title: Validation isn't agreement
activities.summary: Acknowledge another person’s experience without surrendering your own account.

cards.heading: Validate the experience
cards.body: Validation identifies an emotion or understandable impact: “I hear that the canceled plan felt disappointing.” It is different from declaring that every interpretation is fact.

cards.heading: Stay specific and honest
cards.body: If you do not understand, ask: “What about that moment felt hardest?” Avoid “I understand perfectly” if you do not. Do not use “but” to erase the acknowledgement immediately.

cards.heading: Hold two perspectives
cards.body: You can say “I see why you felt left out. I remember the timing differently; can we look at that after I understand more?” You can also disagree with a requested action.

cards.heading: Do not validate abuse
cards.body: You can recognize someone is angry while refusing insults, threats, or control. No one must agree to a conversation that feels unsafe; individual support is an option.

takeaway.question: Which response validates without necessarily agreeing?
options: “I hear that you felt left out.”
takeaway.explanation: It acknowledges the feeling without declaring the disputed account correct.

activities.title: Contempt and its antidote
activities.summary: Interrupt ridicule and replace it with a specific concern or a pause.

cards.heading: Spot the behavior
cards.body: Mocking a voice, name-calling, sneering, or treating someone as beneath you attacks dignity rather than a problem. Note what you actually did, not just that the conversation “got bad.”

cards.heading: Stop rather than add a compliment
cards.body: If you catch yourself, interrupt the behavior: “That was mocking. I am stopping.” An appreciation cannot cancel an insult; the other person may need space and does not owe forgiveness.

cards.heading: Return only if both choose
cards.body: If appropriate, own the action without “but”: “I rolled my eyes while you spoke. That was disrespectful.” Then ask whether a future conversation about the specific issue is welcome.

cards.heading: Protect your boundaries
cards.body: Receiving contempt does not mean you must speak more sweetly to stop it. You can leave a conversation and seek support. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety.

takeaway.question: What is an accountable response after mocking someone?
options: “I mocked you because you made me.”
“Here is a compliment, so forget it.”
takeaway.explanation: Naming and stopping the behavior is more useful than excusing it.

activities.title: Catching defensiveness
activities.summary: Find the piece you can own without accepting an inaccurate or unsafe accusation.

cards.heading: Notice the urge to counterattack
cards.body: When a concern arrives, you may want to list the other person’s mistakes. Pause, breathe, or say “I need a moment.” A pause need not become a promise to resume if doing so is unsafe.

cards.heading: Look for a small true piece
cards.body: You might say “I did forget to call.” Owning this piece does not require accepting “you never care,” taking responsibility for someone else’s conduct, or admitting to something untrue.

cards.heading: Separate impact from intent
cards.body: “I did not intend to leave you waiting, and I see that you waited” can be more accurate than defending intent alone. Ask what practical change would help; decide whether you can agree.

cards.heading: Ask for a different form
cards.body: You can set a limit: “I can discuss the missed call, but not while I am being insulted.” If either person feels unsafe, stop and seek individual support rather than pressing on.

takeaway.question: What does taking partial responsibility mean?
options: Owning a true action without accepting untrue claims.
Proving the other person is more at fault.
takeaway.explanation: An honest, limited acknowledgement is not total blame.

activities.title: Connection Check
activities.summary: Reflect on being known, responsiveness, and room for connection.
activities.intro: Think about the past two weeks from your own perspective. Skip items that do not fit, including when you have not had an opportunity to try. This original educational reflection is not a validated measure, an attachment-style diagnosis, or proof of safety. If fear, coercion or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialist support rather than joint work. Information is stored unencrypted on this device and may be visible to anyone with access. Use a safer device or skip writing if this could put you at risk.

items.text: My partner seems curious about what matters to me lately.
I feel alone with important parts of my daily life.
There is room for my interests or concerns to have changed.
Small attempts to connect seem to go unnoticed.
When I ask for attention, I receive a response even if the answer is “not now.”
I find it difficult to notice or respond to my partner’s invitations to connect.

bands.label: Some moments of connection
bands.narrative: Some answered areas may already feel supported. A score cannot show whether a relationship is safe. You may enjoy noticing one helpful response or choosing a low-pressure question.

bands.label: Room for attention
bands.narrative: Some answered areas may feel distant. Pick one small invitation or individual reflection, rather than trying to change everything at once. Participation and touch are always optional.

bands.label: Consider additional support
bands.narrative: The areas you answered may feel quite lonely or difficult. Individual support may help you identify what you need. Couples support is an option only when freely chosen and safe; if there is fear, coercion or violence, seek individual specialist support first.

activities.title: Bids for connection
activities.summary: Notice small invitations and answer in a way that is honest and kind.

cards.heading: An invitation can be ordinary
cards.body: “Look at this bird,” a sigh after work, or asking to sit together may be an invitation for attention. It is also fine to ask directly rather than hoping someone guesses. Not every glance or message is a bid.

cards.heading: Three possible responses
cards.body: You might turn toward: “That color is amazing.” You might miss it while distracted, or respond sharply. A missed moment is information, not a verdict about the relationship.

cards.heading: A respectful not-now is a response
cards.body: If you are busy, try “I want to hear this; I can listen after dinner if that works.” Follow through only if both still want to. The other person can decline or prefer another time.

cards.heading: Make one invitation clear
cards.body: Try a small, specific ask: “Could we talk for five minutes?” or “Would you look at this with me?” If the answer is no, respect it; connection cannot be demanded.

takeaway.question: Which is a responsive answer when you cannot listen right now?
options: “I cannot listen now; would after dinner work?”
Ignore the invitation without noticing it
Demand they repeat it until you are ready
takeaway.explanation: An honest limit plus an optional alternative can acknowledge the invitation.

activities.title: Attachment in couples
activities.summary: Notice patterns of reaching and making space without assigning fixed types.

cards.heading: Needs can differ by moment
cards.body: When stressed, one person may want closeness while another wants quiet. The same person can want both at different times. These patterns are not fixed personality labels or diagnoses.

cards.heading: The loop can amplify uncertainty
cards.body: One person asks repeatedly for reassurance; the other takes more space; the first asks again. Either can notice the loop without assuming equal responsibility for harmful behavior or control.

cards.heading: Make the need specific
cards.body: Instead of “You never care,” try “I am unsettled; would a five-minute check-in be possible?” Instead of disappearing, if safe, try “I need quiet tonight; I can check whether tomorrow works.”

cards.heading: No pattern excuses harm
cards.body: Fear, coercion, threats or violence are not attachment-style differences to solve together. Seek individual specialist support; no one owes closeness or a return to conversation.

takeaway.question: How should attachment ideas be used here?
options: As flexible clues about needs, not labels or diagnoses
As proof that someone is permanently one type
As an excuse for controlling behavior
takeaway.explanation: Context changes, and labels cannot determine what a person needs.

activities.title: Softening
activities.summary: Find a more precise feeling and ask for something small, if safe.

cards.heading: Anger may carry information
cards.body: Irritation can accompany hurt, loneliness, fear, or a crossed boundary. It can also be an appropriate signal of mistreatment; you do not have to replace it with a gentler feeling.

cards.heading: Try a three-part sentence
cards.body: If it is safe and you want to share, use “When ___ happened, I felt ___; would you be willing to ___?” Example: “When plans changed without a message, I felt left out; could you text me next time?”

cards.heading: Be specific, not exposed
cards.body: You choose how much to reveal. “I need a little quiet” is enough; you do not have to disclose a trauma, demonstrate vulnerability, or accept touch to connect.

cards.heading: A request is not control
cards.body: The other person can say no. If they do, consider an alternative or a boundary within your control. If it is unsafe to express a need, seek individual support rather than practicing disclosure together.

takeaway.question: Which is a specific, optional request?
options: “I felt left out when plans changed; would you message me next time?”
“You must prove you care right now.”
“I should reveal everything even if I feel unsafe.”
takeaway.explanation: The request gives useful information without demanding agreement.

activities.title: Staying curious about each other
activities.summary: Update what you know instead of treating a partner as a finished story.

cards.heading: People change in small ways
cards.body: A favorite way to unwind, a work worry, or a hope for the weekend can shift. Familiarity does not guarantee current knowledge, even in a long relationship.

cards.heading: Ask an open, bounded question
cards.body: Try “What has been taking more energy than I realize lately?” or “What is something small you are looking forward to?” Invite a pass and avoid pressing for sensitive details.

cards.heading: Listen for correction
cards.body: Summarize: “It sounds as though your new schedule is tiring.” Then ask “Did I get that right?” Let the person correct the summary without having to defend their preference.

cards.heading: Remember with permission
cards.body: If welcome, follow up later: “You mentioned a difficult meeting; would you like to tell me how it went?” The goal is attention, not scoring answers or proving how well you know someone.

takeaway.question: What makes a curiosity question respectful?
options: It allows a pass and accepts correction
It demands a complete personal history
It awards points for the right answer
takeaway.explanation: Curiosity is an invitation rather than an examination.

activities.title: Being reachable
activities.summary: Practice small, realistic responses rather than promising constant availability.

cards.heading: Availability has limits
cards.body: Being emotionally reachable does not mean answering immediately, dropping work, providing therapy, or being available around the clock. A clear limit can be kinder than a promise you cannot keep.

cards.heading: Acknowledge the attempt
cards.body: Try “I hear that this matters.” Then ask: “Do you want listening, help thinking, or some space?” If you cannot offer it now, say so plainly.

cards.heading: Make a realistic offer
cards.body: Offer an achievable window only if you can: “I have ten minutes after I finish this task; would that help?” Follow up if you offered, and allow the other person to decline.

cards.heading: Notice what works
cards.body: Afterward, ask whether your response helped, without insisting on praise. If the answer is no, listen or revise. Each person is responsible for their own boundaries and support network.

takeaway.question: What is a realistic way to be reachable?
options: Acknowledge the request and offer only the time you can give
Promise to be available at all times
Decide the other person needs advice without asking
takeaway.explanation: Reachability includes honest limits and respect for the other person’s choice.

activities.title: Desire differences are normal
activities.summary: Differences in interest are information, not a verdict about either person.

cards.heading: There is no required frequency
cards.body: People differ in whether, when, and how they want sexual or physical closeness. Desire can change with circumstances or over a lifetime, and a person may not want sex at all. A difference is not proof that someone is broken, unloving, or withholding.

cards.heading: Name the impact, not a culprit
cards.body: Different preferences can bring disappointment, relief, worry, or no distress. Notice your own feelings separately from a claim about your partner. Try: “I miss feeling wanted, and I want us both to be free to choose.” Do not assume the other person shares your interpretation.

cards.heading: Protect the right to choose
cards.body: An invitation is not a request that must be granted. Neither partner owes sex, touch, an explanation, or a replacement activity. A no, uncertainty, silence, or a change of mind means stop; enthusiasm cannot be negotiated into existence.

cards.heading: Find the actual question
cards.body: Ask yourself what you miss: play, tenderness, reassurance, erotic interest, or quiet time? Then consider ways to meet that need that do not require another person to override a boundary. A shared conversation is optional and appropriate only when both feel safe and freely agree.

takeaway.question: Which response respects a difference in desire?
options: Ask about needs while accepting that either person can decline
takeaway.explanation: Desire differences can be explored without setting a quota or overriding choice.

activities.title: Spontaneous vs. responsive desire
activities.summary: Recognize different ways interest can appear without treating a pattern as a rule.

cards.heading: Two possible patterns
cards.body: Some people notice interest before any intimate context; others sometimes notice it after feeling relaxed, connected, or engaged in something they already welcome. These are descriptions, not fixed types, and neither is more mature or more valid.

cards.heading: Response is not a promise
cards.body: Responsive desire does not mean someone should start an activity they do not want to see if desire appears. They may prefer no activity at all. A comfortable context can support choice, but it cannot create an obligation or guarantee interest.

cards.heading: Notice variation
cards.body: Consider a recent moment when you did want some form of closeness. What was happening beforehand? Consider a time you did not. Sleep, privacy, workload, mood, medication, relationship context, and many other factors may matter differently from day to day.

cards.heading: Make room for uncertainty
cards.body: A useful answer can be “not now,” “I do not know,” or “only a conversation.” Ask for what you want rather than testing another person. If the response is anything other than a freely given yes to that specific activity, do not proceed.

takeaway.question: What does responsive desire imply?
options: A person owes their partner a trial of touch
Desire can sometimes emerge in a welcome context, but never has to
A person has one permanent desire type
takeaway.explanation: Context may matter, but an activity is optional from the start and throughout.

activities.title: Accelerators and brakes
activities.summary: Map conditions that make closeness more or less appealing to you.

cards.heading: A practical metaphor
cards.body: An accelerator is something that can support interest; a brake is something that can make interest less likely. The same situation can affect people differently. These are observations, not levers one person can use to get the other to agree.

cards.heading: Look beyond romance
cards.body: A sense of privacy, time to decompress, feeling respected, sensory preferences, and mental load might affect interest. A person may also have no identifiable reason. Make two lists of your own examples rather than guessing what works for someone else.

cards.heading: A brake is useful information
cards.body: Pain, exhaustion, resentment, interruptions, or worry can be a reason to stop or choose another activity. Removing a brake is not a bargain that earns sex. If pain is a concern, stop the painful activity and consider a qualified clinician.

cards.heading: Try one low-stakes adjustment
cards.body: If you wish, choose an adjustment that is useful on its own, such as protecting twenty minutes of quiet or sharing a chore more fairly. Later ask yourself whether it helped your wellbeing. Do not measure success by whether sex happened.

takeaway.question: If a brake is removed, what follows?
options: Consent is still needed, and either person can still say no
The person must explain any remaining reluctance
takeaway.explanation: A more comfortable context never obliges an intimate activity.

activities.title: Rebuilding affection after distance or betrayal
activities.summary: Consider connection at a pace that does not assume touch or forgiveness.

cards.heading: Distance may make sense
cards.body: After conflict, a health change, or a breach of trust, closeness may feel complicated. There is no timetable for wanting contact and no exercise that repairs trust on its own. Addressing harm and respecting boundaries matter more than demonstrating affection.

cards.heading: Connection has many forms
cards.body: For some, sharing a cup of tea, a kind word, sitting nearby, or having personal space feels connecting. Touch is only one option and can be unwelcome. Ask what would feel comfortable rather than assuming a gesture is harmless.

cards.heading: Ask about this moment
cards.body: If both people want a gesture, name it specifically: “Would you like to sit next to me for five minutes?” Accept “no,” “not sure,” or no answer without sulking or bargaining. A yes to one gesture is not consent to another.

cards.heading: Let the person set the pace
cards.body: A person can stop or change their mind at any time, even after saying yes. Avoid turning affectionate moments into a test or a route to sex. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, skip joint exercises and seek specialist individual support.

takeaway.question: What is a safe starting assumption?
options: Connection might include no touch, and either person may stop
Affection is proof that past harm is resolved
takeaway.explanation: Connection can be nonphysical, and choice remains active.

activities.title: When to see a doctor or sex therapist
activities.summary: Find appropriate support for physical discomfort or ongoing questions.

cards.heading: Pain is not a task to push through
cards.body: If a sexual or physical activity hurts, stop that activity. You do not need to tolerate pain to maintain a relationship or complete an exercise. Pain or a change in comfort is a reason to consider talking with a qualified clinician, even if it is intermittent.

cards.heading: Prepare for an appointment
cards.body: If you want, note when the discomfort occurs, what you have already tried, relevant health changes or medications, and your questions. You can decide what to disclose and ask the clinician to explain options. This lesson cannot identify a cause or recommend treatment.

cards.heading: Choose support that fits
cards.body: A licensed clinician can help explore physical concerns. A qualified sex therapist may help with questions about desire, communication, or distress; individual support is an option. Ask about credentials, approach, cost, and whether the provider respects consent and diverse identities.

cards.heading: Safety comes first
cards.body: If someone pressures you, controls your choices, or you are afraid, do not use couples work as the first response. Consider contacting a specialist violence or sexual-assault support service individually, in a way that is safe for you. You decide what to do next.

takeaway.question: What is an appropriate response to pain during an activity?
options: Stop the painful activity and consider speaking with a qualified clinician
Assume it will resolve without attention
takeaway.explanation: Pain is not something anyone needs to endure for intimacy.

activities.title: Connection without losing yourself
activities.summary: Build partnership while preserving each person’s independent relationships.

cards.heading: A partnership is not a merger
cards.body: Family of origin, chosen family, friends and community can remain important. Building a “we” need not mean choosing a partner over everyone else, accepting mistreatment, or surrendering individual relationships.

cards.heading: Name the actual conflict
cards.body: Instead of “your family always comes first,” identify a concrete situation: “The visit was planned for Saturday before I was asked; I need a say in my availability.” Avoid guessing what a relative intended.

cards.heading: Joint and individual choices
cards.body: A shared home or joint hosting plan may require agreement from those affected. Each person can also choose their own contact and decline participation. A partner cannot set limits for another adult as a loyalty test.

cards.heading: Make room for both
cards.body: If safe, ask what each person values and can freely choose. One person may attend a family meal while the other stays home, without demanding that either prove devotion.

takeaway.question: Which choice supports connection and autonomy?
options: Require both partners to cut off relatives.
Agree about joint hosting while each chooses their own contact.
Plan a visit for everyone without asking.
takeaway.explanation: Shared decisions and individual relationships both deserve respect.

activities.title: Flexible boundaries and limits
activities.summary: Create a limit about your own participation, not a rule controlling someone else.

cards.heading: A boundary names your action
cards.body: “If a conversation turns to insults, I will leave the call” describes an action you can take. “You must never talk to your sibling” attempts to control another person’s relationship.

cards.heading: Be specific and proportionate
cards.body: Name the situation, limit and next step: “I cannot host overnight this month; I can meet for lunch if that works.” You can decline entirely, and need not explain more than you want.

cards.heading: Flexibility is chosen
cards.body: A limit may change for an emergency or new information, but exceptions require your consent. Respecting someone’s limit also means not repeatedly pressing after a no.

cards.heading: Safety changes the plan
cards.body: If setting a limit may provoke threats, stalking, control or violence, do not confront the person through a joint exercise. Seek individual support from a domestic abuse specialist and use a safe device if possible.

takeaway.question: Which is a boundary rather than a demand to control someone?
options: “If insults continue, I will leave the visit.”
“You may never contact your friend again.”
“Give me your phone to prove loyalty.”
takeaway.explanation: A boundary describes what you will do and respects the other person’s autonomy.

activities.title: Loyalty binds
activities.summary: Handle competing expectations without forcing a choice between important people.

cards.heading: The squeeze
cards.body: A relative asks for frequent visits while your partner wants quieter weekends. You may care about both relationships and still have limits on time, money, energy or accessibility.

cards.heading: Untangle the requests
cards.body: Write the requests separately. Ask what you can offer voluntarily and what another person can decide for themselves. Do not make promises on someone else’s behalf or share their private reasons.

cards.heading: Speak from your position
cards.body: Try “I can visit Sunday afternoon, but I cannot host overnight.” A partner can choose whether to attend. Declining an invitation is not disloyalty, and neither person must use the other as an excuse.

cards.heading: Expect feelings, not compliance
cards.body: Someone may feel disappointed even when the limit is respectful. Acknowledge the feeling without promising to change your answer; revisit only if you want to and it is safe.

takeaway.question: What helps when two people make competing demands?
options: Promise on behalf of your partner.
Clarify what you can offer without sharing another person’s private reasons.
takeaway.explanation: You can acknowledge disappointment without deciding for someone else.

activities.title: Phones, social media and attention
activities.summary: Negotiate attention and consent without monitoring devices.

cards.heading: Different uses, different needs
cards.body: A phone can be work, accessibility, caregiving, support or leisure. Rather than assume disinterest, ask about a specific interruption and what kind of attention would be welcome.

cards.heading: Request a small window
cards.body: Try “Would you like ten minutes together after dinner, with optional phone breaks?” Either person may decline or need a device nearby for care, safety or access.

cards.heading: Ask before posting
cards.body: Discuss permission before sharing another person’s image, location, message or personal news. Consent to one post is not consent to future posts; removal requests deserve respect.

cards.heading: Privacy is not a problem to solve
cards.body: Do not require passwords, location tracking, device checks or access to private communications as proof of trust. If someone monitors or restricts device use, consider individual specialist support on a safer device.

takeaway.question: Which technology agreement respects autonomy?
options: Ask before posting a photo and allow a no.
Ban all devices regardless of accessibility or care.
takeaway.explanation: Consent and realistic access needs matter more than surveillance.

activities.summary: Notice tendencies to avoid, escalate, listen, repair, and work through differences.
activities.intro: Think about disagreements in the past month. This original, unvalidated reflection describes tendencies, not fixed conflict types, a diagnosis, or a safety screen. High scores indicate more concern, not a verdict on either person. Stop if you wish. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support rather than couples activities.

activities.title: Solvable vs. perpetual problems
activities.summary: Choose a practical trial or a way to live with a recurring difference.

cards.heading: Two kinds of question
cards.body: A practical problem has a defined target, such as who buys groceries this week. An ongoing difference, such as wanting different amounts of social time, may return even after a good plan. Either can matter.

cards.heading: Test the label
cards.body: Ask: “Could a specific, acceptable action resolve this particular instance?” If yes, brainstorm a small trial. If deeper preferences or values keep recurring, allow for a continuing difference. The label can change.

cards.heading: Handle a mixed problem
cards.body: For different sleep schedules, a practical trial might be headphones after 10 p.m.; the ongoing difference is the preferred bedtime. Revisit whether the trial works without demanding identical preferences.

cards.heading: Safety is not a compromise category
cards.body: Threats, coercion, or violence are not “perpetual differences” to manage together. Stop couples work and prioritize individual safety and specialized support.

takeaway.question: Which issue is most clearly a practical problem to test?
options: Deciding who picks up groceries on Tuesday.
Making two people have identical social needs.
takeaway.explanation: A concrete task has a target and a way to check a trial.

activities.title: Repair attempts
activities.summary: Use a short pause, acknowledgement, or reset without demanding immediate forgiveness.

cards.heading: A repair is an invitation
cards.body: A repair attempt interrupts an unhelpful exchange: “That came out sharply; I want to try again,” or “I need a break.” It does not guarantee that the other person feels ready to continue.

cards.heading: Match the action to the moment
cards.body: If you interrupted, stop and invite the person to finish. If you insulted, name the insult and stop it; do not use humor or touch to cover it. If overwhelmed, pause without chasing the other person.

cards.heading: Receiving is optional
cards.body: “I hear your apology; I need time” is a valid response. Do not insist that a partner accept a repair, give affection, or resume immediately.

cards.heading: Look beyond the phrase
cards.body: A repeated apology without a change in behavior may not repair harm. If there is fear, coercion, or violence, a repair phrase is not a safety plan; seek individual specialized support.

takeaway.question: After an insult, which response is a repair attempt?
options: “I insulted you; that was wrong. I will stop.”
“I apologized, so you must move on.”
takeaway.explanation: It acknowledges the action and stops it without demanding forgiveness.

activities.title: Compromise without losing yourself
activities.summary: Separate non-negotiable boundaries from flexible details, then test an agreement.

cards.heading: Start separately
cards.body: Write down what you need to protect—such as sleep, control of your own body, or a spending limit you can afford. A boundary is about what you will do, not a rule you can force on another person.

cards.heading: Find flexible details
cards.body: List details you could adjust without violating that boundary: timing, duration, location, or who does a task. Do not label someone’s safety or consent as a bargaining chip.

cards.heading: Propose a small experiment
cards.body: For instance, “Could we try visitors ending by 9 on work nights for two weeks?” Both can propose changes or decline. Record the action, owner, timing, and a check-in only if both choose.

cards.heading: Review, do not coerce
cards.body: At the check-in, ask what worked and what did not. Revise or end the trial. A refusal to compromise about safety, bodily autonomy, or dignity is legitimate.

takeaway.question: Which element belongs in a workable trial?
options: An action, a duration, and agreement by both.
A demand that neither person may decline.
An exchange of one person’s safety for convenience.
takeaway.explanation: A limited, mutually chosen trial can be reviewed without erasing boundaries.

activities.title: The dreams inside gridlock
activities.summary: Explore the values underneath a recurring disagreement without promising a solution.

cards.heading: Get specific about the stuck point
cards.body: Instead of “we disagree about family,” name the recurring choice, such as how often to host relatives. Each person may experience the same choice differently.

cards.heading: Ask about meaning, not evidence
cards.body: “What does hosting mean to you?” may reveal belonging, rest, financial stress, or a memory. Do not assume that a value explains away a harmful action.

cards.heading: Reflect before negotiating
cards.body: Try: “I hear that hosting helps you feel connected; did I get that?” Then switch if both wish. Understanding another value does not require adopting it or changing a boundary.

cards.heading: Look for a narrow experiment
cards.body: Maybe one gathering is shorter, or one partner attends separately. Either can decline, and some differences may remain unresolved. If fear or coercion is present, do not use this as a couples exercise.

takeaway.question: Why ask about the meaning underneath a disagreement?
options: To discover what matters to each person before considering options.
To prove a boundary is negotiable.
takeaway.explanation: Curiosity can reveal values without creating an obligation to agree.

activities.title: Accepting influence
activities.summary: Take another person’s perspective into account without surrendering your own judgment.

cards.heading: Influence is a choice, not compliance
cards.body: Listening for useful information means considering a perspective, not agreeing automatically. Both people retain the right to disagree, set limits, or stop.

cards.heading: Name what changes your thinking
cards.body: Try: “I had not considered the cost of a late pickup. I could move it earlier.” Be specific about the point you heard instead of promising more than you can deliver.

cards.heading: Offer your own constraint
cards.body: Add “I cannot leave work before 5; could we try 5:30?” A real agreement needs both people’s voluntary consent and a workable plan.

cards.heading: Notice unequal power
cards.body: If one person is afraid to say no, more influence is not the goal. Prioritize individual safety and specialized support; do not use negotiation to manage coercion or violence.

takeaway.question: What does accepting influence mean?
options: Considering a valid point while keeping your own boundaries.
Ignoring a disagreement to preserve peace.
takeaway.explanation: Listening can change a plan without requiring either person to give up consent.

activities.title: What forgiveness is and isn't
activities.summary: Separate an optional internal choice from excusing, trusting, or reconnecting.

cards.heading: There is no obligation
cards.body: Some people describe forgiveness as changing their relationship to resentment; others do not find the word useful. You are not required to forgive to heal, be a good partner, or complete these activities.

cards.heading: Four different decisions
cards.body: Forgiving, if you choose it, is not the same as saying the behavior was acceptable. It also does not automatically restore trust, remove consequences, or require reconciliation or contact.

cards.heading: Boundaries still count
cards.body: You can say “I do not want to discuss that tonight” or choose distance while deciding how you feel. A boundary describes what you will do; it is not a tool for controlling the other person.

cards.heading: Safety is not a forgiveness project
cards.body: If someone frightens, controls, threatens, or harms you, do not use a joint activity to make the situation feel normal. Seek an individual domestic abuse specialist using a device you consider safe.

takeaway.question: Which choice can coexist with forgiveness, if someone freely chooses it?
options: Maintaining a boundary or ending contact
takeaway.explanation: Forgiveness, boundaries, and trust are separate decisions.

activities.title: Resentment as an unmet need
activities.summary: Use resentment as information, not a verdict or an instruction.

cards.heading: Find the particular moment
cards.body: “I resent everything” is hard to act on. Choose a smaller example: “When I covered the appointment alone, I felt overlooked.” You do not have to minimize repeated or serious harm to pick one example.

cards.heading: Look for the need underneath
cards.body: Ask what mattered: fairness, rest, acknowledgment, reliability, or choice. Resentment may point to an unmet need, but it can also signal an ongoing boundary violation or danger.

cards.heading: Decide who can act
cards.body: Some needs can be addressed independently, such as arranging time off. Others require a voluntary request: “Would you take the next appointment?” A request is not an agreement until the other person accepts it.

cards.heading: Notice what happens next
cards.body: If an agreed action is repeatedly missed, reassess the agreement and your own options rather than treating your resentment as the sole problem. Seek support where the situation feels unsafe.

takeaway.question: A useful question about a recurring resentment is:
options: “What need or boundary might this be pointing to?”
“How can I force myself never to feel it?”
“How can I make the other person agree?”
takeaway.explanation: The feeling may provide information; you still choose what to do with it.

activities.title: Forgiveness is a process
activities.summary: Allow feelings to change without treating forgiveness as a required destination.

cards.heading: Nonlinear does not mean failure
cards.body: A hurt can feel quieter one week and vivid the next. A reminder is not proof you are back at the beginning, and you need not measure yourself against someone else’s timeline.

cards.heading: Distinguish old and ongoing
cards.body: Ask: “Is this a memory of something that stopped, or is something similar still happening?” An ongoing pattern may call for a boundary or outside support, not an exercise in letting go.

cards.heading: Use a review, not a deadline
cards.body: Choose a time to notice what has changed in your needs, sleep, boundaries, or access to support. The purpose is information, not declaring the hurt over or promising forgiveness.

cards.heading: Pick your own outcome
cards.body: You might choose forgiveness, uncertainty, distance, practical repair, or ending the relationship. You can revise your choice. A trustworthy response respects that autonomy.

takeaway.question: If the same hurtful behavior is still happening, what is a helpful next question?
options: “What boundary or support might I need?”
“How do I prove it did not matter?”
takeaway.explanation: Ongoing behavior deserves attention rather than a forced closure date.

activities.title: Forgiving yourself
activities.summary: Take responsibility for your own choices without turning shame into a life sentence.

cards.heading: Describe a choice precisely
cards.body: Replace “I am terrible” with a specific action: “I canceled without telling them.” If someone harmed or controlled you, responsibility for their behavior belongs to them, not to you.

cards.heading: Face the effect without a defense
cards.body: Notice the likely impact and what you do not know. An apology can name the action and impact, without “but” or a demand that the other person make you feel better.

cards.heading: Make amends where appropriate
cards.body: Ask if an offer would be welcome; accept no. Choose a realistic change such as sending notice earlier next time. Sometimes respecting distance is the most appropriate action.

cards.heading: Practice a humane next step
cards.body: Guilt can point to an action to repair; global shame can keep you stuck. Try: “I can regret that choice and still take a useful step.” You do not need someone else’s forgiveness to take responsibility.

takeaway.question: What is a constructive self-forgiveness practice?
options: Name a specific choice, acknowledge impact, and take a feasible step
Insist the other person absolve you
Take responsibility for someone else’s abuse
takeaway.explanation: Accountability and self-compassion can coexist without demanding a response.

activities.title: Why reactions can linger
activities.summary: Understand reminders without treating them as a diagnosis.

cards.heading: A reminder can arrive unexpectedly
cards.body: A song, a delayed reply, or an ordinary place may bring the event back to mind. Your reaction can vary from day to day; neither intensity nor calm proves what decision you should make.

cards.heading: Name the present moment
cards.body: If a reminder arrives, notice what is happening now: “I heard that song and my chest tightened.” Look around, feel your feet on the floor, or name three ordinary objects. Skip any technique that makes you feel worse.

cards.heading: Separate comfort from investigation
cards.body: Ask what is needed in the next ten minutes: water, space, sleep, a trusted person, or writing a question for later. You do not need to chase every detail to take your feelings seriously.

cards.heading: Get additional support
cards.body: If intrusive thoughts, sleep disruption or distress are persistent or interfere with daily life, consider an individual mental health professional. If you feel controlled or afraid, contact a domestic abuse specialist from a device you consider safe.

takeaway.question: A reminder appears while you are trying to work. What is a useful first step?
options: Force yourself to settle the relationship today
Notice the reminder and choose a small present-focused support
Demand immediate access to someone else’s phone
takeaway.explanation: Settling first creates room for choice; it does not minimize the hurt.

activities.title: A flexible map, not a recovery timetable
activities.summary: Consider stabilization, accountability, and future choices without a prescribed sequence.

cards.heading: Start where you are
cards.body: Some people first need sleep, practical support, or distance. Others want to understand what happened. There is no universal sequence or deadline, and a relationship may end.

cards.heading: Accountability is observable
cards.body: If the involved person chooses to repair, accountability can mean acknowledging specific actions and their impact without blaming the hurt person, making realistic commitments, and following through. A statement of regret alone does not establish trust.

cards.heading: Look at the pattern over time
cards.body: If both freely want to continue, they can notice whether agreed actions happen, whether either can say no, and whether hard topics can be paused. Set a modest review date rather than demanding certainty today.

cards.heading: Bring in the right help
cards.body: An individual therapist can support either person’s decisions. A qualified couples therapist may help when both want to participate and there is no coercion or violence. If there is fear or control, prioritize independent specialist support instead.

takeaway.question: Which statement best describes this map?
options: Everyone must reach the same final stage
It offers possible tasks, not a deadline or a requirement to stay
A lower score means an affair is resolved
takeaway.explanation: People move differently, and safety and choice are more important than a schedule.

activities.title: Questions with a purpose
activities.summary: Choose questions that support decisions while limiting unwanted detail.

cards.heading: Begin with the reason
cards.body: Before asking, complete: “I need this information to decide ___.” Questions about relevant health, current contact, and practical boundaries may be more useful for decisions than an exhaustive replay.

cards.heading: Agree on a container
cards.body: Only if both already know the relevant facts and freely agree, choose one question, a time limit, and a way to stop. Either person may decline details or choose to discuss them with an individual professional first.

cards.heading: Avoid detail you cannot unhear
cards.body: Ask at the level you actually want. For example, “What contact is ongoing?” may be more useful than asking for a minute-by-minute description. You can change your mind, stop, and revisit a question later.

cards.heading: Make health decisions independently
cards.body: If sexual health is a concern, consult a qualified clinician about testing, timing, and protection. You can seek care without waiting for a partner’s permission or for a joint discussion.

takeaway.question: What makes a question more likely to be useful?
options: It supports a decision and respects the desired level of detail
It guarantees the answer will feel comfortable
takeaway.explanation: Purpose and control over detail can help reduce unnecessary overwhelm.

activities.title: Responding without defensiveness
activities.summary: For someone who broke trust: acknowledge impact while respecting boundaries.

cards.heading: Pause your defense
cards.body: Hearing hurt can bring shame or an urge to correct every detail. Take a breath. You can say, “I want to understand; may I take a moment?” A pause is not permission to disappear or demand reassurance.

cards.heading: Own the action
cards.body: Try: “I chose to hide that contact. I understand that discovering it changed how safe our agreements felt. I am sorry.” Avoid “I am sorry you feel that way” or explanations that shift responsibility.

cards.heading: Offer a specific next action
cards.body: Instead of asking for instant trust, name something feasible: “I will tell you if unavoidable work contact occurs, in the way we agree.” Offer, do not impose; the other person may need something different or no discussion.

cards.heading: Respect their response
cards.body: A hurt person may be angry, uncertain, or unwilling to talk. They do not owe comfort or forgiveness. If either person feels threatened or controlled, stop joint work and seek individual specialist help.

takeaway.question: Which response takes responsibility without demanding forgiveness?
options: “I hid the contact, and I am sorry; would you like to hear one change I can make?”
“I said sorry, so you need to move on.”
“I did it because you were distant.”
takeaway.explanation: Ownership names the choice and leaves the other person free to respond.

activities.title: Context is not an excuse
activities.summary: Explore relationship context without assigning blame for someone else’s choices.

cards.heading: Two questions, not one
cards.body: “What conditions were present?” and “Who chose the behavior?” are different questions. Loneliness, conflict, or opportunity may be relevant context; they do not make another person responsible for a breach of trust.

cards.heading: Choose what is worth examining
cards.body: A person might notice they avoided difficult conversations or ignored their own boundaries. Examine your own choices without treating a partner’s actions as your fault. No one is obligated to search for their contribution.

cards.heading: Make a small forward-looking request
cards.body: If both people freely want to discuss the relationship, replace a global verdict with a specific request: “Can we set aside ten minutes on Sunday to talk about our schedules?” A request can be declined or renegotiated.

cards.heading: Do not use context to bypass safety
cards.body: Threats, intimidation, coercive control and violence are not mutual communication problems. Do not use a joint exercise to fix them; contact an individual domestic abuse specialist when safe.

takeaway.question: How can you examine context without excusing a betrayal?
options: Make the hurt person responsible for the choice
Distinguish relationship conditions from the individual’s decision
Assume both people share equal responsibility
takeaway.explanation: Understanding context does not transfer responsibility.

activities.title: Money carries meaning
activities.summary: Separate practical decisions from the meanings and constraints around them.

cards.heading: The bill and the story
cards.body: A bill is a practical problem; it may also bring up fear, anger, or a sense of being alone. Money can simply be scarce. Treat numbers and feelings as different information rather than evidence that either person is bad.

cards.heading: Name the decision
cards.body: Instead of “you never care about money,” try “The electricity bill is due Friday; can we decide who will check it?” Describe one decision and its timing before interpreting motives or arguing about character.

cards.heading: Ask about meaning
cards.body: A purchase may represent rest to one person and uncertainty to another. If both want to discuss it, ask “What matters to you about this?” and accept “I am not ready to talk.” Meaning does not erase an action’s real impact.

cards.heading: Make a small test
cards.body: If both choose to discuss it, agree on a limited next action, its owner and a review date. Each can consider what to revisit next week; no account details or promise to agree are required.

takeaway.question: What is a useful first step when an ordinary bill becomes an argument?
options: Identify the specific decision and ask what matters to each person.
Assume the other person is irresponsible.
takeaway.explanation: A concrete decision leaves room for feelings and constraints without demanding private information.

activities.title: Your money story
activities.summary: Notice messages about money without treating them as fixed identities.

cards.heading: Recall a message
cards.body: Think of a sentence you absorbed about money: “Save everything” or “We can always manage.” It may have helped in one situation without fitting your life now; you do not need to revisit painful details.

cards.heading: Connect past and present
cards.body: Notice one trigger, such as an unexpected charge, and your reaction. Ask what it may be protecting: stability, independence, generosity, or another value. Your history can explain a reaction without excusing harmful behavior.

cards.heading: Preference or constraint?
cards.body: Labels such as “spender” and “saver” can hide caregiving, disability, debt, unequal income or a lack of available choices. Describe a behavior and context instead of assigning a permanent personality.

cards.heading: Choose what to keep
cards.body: Choose one inherited rule to keep, revise or question. If sharing feels safe, offer only what you want: “Unexpected costs make me anxious; advance notice would help.” The other person may have a different story.

takeaway.question: Which statement keeps a money story open to change?
options: “I learned to save during uncertainty, and I can reconsider that rule.”
“My history proves all spending is unsafe.”
takeaway.explanation: A learned rule can be useful, limited, or revised without labeling either person.

activities.title: Privacy, secrecy and financial control
activities.summary: Distinguish privacy from broken shared agreements and coercive control.

cards.heading: Privacy is not proof of harm
cards.body: People may reasonably keep financial details private. No one owes a partner passwords, account access, balances or a complete financial history. Agreeing to a shared expense differs from surrendering privacy.

cards.heading: Notice an actual commitment
cards.body: When an agreed shared bill is not covered or a material shared obligation is concealed, the practical impact may be real. Describe the specific agreement and effect; do not turn every private purchase into a betrayal.

cards.heading: Control is not a budgeting style
cards.body: Taking someone’s wages, withholding necessities, threatening consequences for ordinary choices, or monitoring every transaction can be financial abuse. The person experiencing it is not responsible for fixing another person’s control.

cards.heading: Put safety first
cards.body: If fear, coercion or violence is present, do not confront the person through a joint exercise or require disclosure. A domestic abuse specialist can help individually using a safer device; in immediate danger contact local emergency services if safe.

takeaway.question: Which response respects privacy and safety?
options: Discuss a shared commitment voluntarily; seek individual specialist help if control is present.
takeaway.explanation: Consent and practical agreements can coexist; control calls for individual support, not joint problem-solving.

activities.title: Shared, separate or hybrid
activities.summary: Compare arrangements by agency and practical needs rather than one ideal.

cards.heading: No universal setup
cards.body: Some people keep resources separate, pool them, or combine shared expenses with individual resources. None is inherently fair or safe; income, caregiving, health and local circumstances can differ.

cards.heading: Discuss functions, not passwords
cards.body: If both freely agree, identify a shared expense, how it is handled, who follows through, and what happens if circumstances change. A planning conversation does not require access to someone else’s accounts.

cards.heading: Check actual agency
cards.body: Ask whether each person can access necessities, make ordinary choices, question a plan and decline changes without retaliation. A supposedly shared system can be controlling if only one person has meaningful access.

cards.heading: Try and review
cards.body: Choose a small, reversible arrangement only if both consent. Write what is being tried and when to review it. For personal questions about obligations, taxes, benefits or financial products, seek independent qualified advice.

takeaway.question: What matters more than a particular account structure?
options: Both people can make choices and review a voluntary plan.
One person should control the plan.
takeaway.explanation: Fairness and agency matter more than the arrangement’s label.

activities.title: My money autobiography
activities.summary: Trace a formative money message and decide whether it still serves you.
activities.intro: Work alone; use broad descriptions rather than names, account details or amounts. Skip anything you do not want to record.

steps.prompt: Recall one early money message or experience. What did it teach you?
What current situation brings it to mind, and what feeling or physical signal do you notice?
What circumstances are different now, including resources or responsibilities?
Name one rule to keep, revise or question, and one small action you could take.

activities.summary: Compare how a small shared responsibility could work.
activities.intro: Individually sketch options. This is educational, not financial or legal advice; no account details are needed.

List possible arrangements, including separate contributions, pooled resources, a hybrid, or another approach.
