activities.title: The invisible mental load
activities.summary: Break a household job into noticing, planning, doing and following up.

cards.heading: A task has hidden stages
cards.body: Dinner is not only cooking. Someone notices food is low, checks preferences and dietary needs, plans meals, shops, cooks and handles leftovers. The visible chore is only part of the work.

cards.heading: Ownership includes remembering
cards.body: “Tell me what to do” can leave one person as project manager. For one task, name who notices, plans, executes and checks completion, including who handles exceptions. These stages can be split if both agree.

cards.heading: Count context, not only minutes
cards.body: Work schedules, physical access, disability, energy, childcare and paid work shape available capacity. Fairness may mean different contributions and rest for each person, rather than a perfect 50/50 count.

cards.heading: Make a small transfer
cards.body: Choose a recurring task, agree what “done” means, transfer necessary information with consent, and name a backup. One person might own a grocery trip from list through putting food away. Review after a week.

takeaway.question: What makes a task transfer more than helping on request?
options: An agreed owner handles planning and follow-through, with a backup.
The usual planner keeps reminding the other.
takeaway.explanation: Clear ownership covers noticing and follow-through while allowing an agreed backup.

activities.title: Making room for partnership
activities.summary: Protect rest and connection without putting a relationship above safety or individual needs.

cards.heading: Start with capacity
cards.body: Connection can be hard when someone is exhausted or carrying invisible work. Instead of adding a date to an overloaded schedule, identify what can be paused, shared, simplified or supported by others.

cards.heading: Connection can be small
cards.body: Ask what contact is welcome: a few quiet minutes, sharing tea, or being left alone to rest. Each person can decline touch, a conversation or an outing without having to justify it.

cards.heading: Not “couple first” at any cost
cards.body: Children need safe, responsive care, and adults need autonomy and support. Protecting partnership time never means ignoring a child’s urgent needs or pressuring someone into closeness.

cards.heading: Try one realistic window
cards.body: If both want, choose ten minutes and a backup for interruptions. If it does not happen, treat that as information about capacity rather than evidence that someone does not care.

takeaway.question: When someone is exhausted, what is a practical first step?
options: Insist on a demanding weekly date.
Ask what can be simplified or shared and what connection is welcome.
takeaway.explanation: Rest and safe care make voluntary connection more feasible.

activities.title: Different parenting styles, shared care
activities.summary: Discuss care differences without silencing concerns or overriding a child’s wellbeing.

cards.heading: Separate values from tactics
cards.body: Caregivers may both value safety and respect but prefer different bedtime routines. Ask what each hopes a child will learn or feel before debating the tactic.

cards.heading: Respond to immediate needs
cards.body: If a child is at risk or needs comfort, respond to their safety now. A “united front” is not a reason to tolerate frightening, degrading or harmful treatment or stay silent about a concern.

cards.heading: Disagree away from the child when possible
cards.body: For a non-urgent disagreement, compare observations in private: “I noticed bedtime took longer; what did you see?” Seek age-appropriate input from a child where suitable, without making them choose sides.

cards.heading: Make a testable plan
cards.body: Select one routine and a response each can carry out, a backup and a review date. If concerns about a child’s safety, development or wellbeing persist, consult an appropriate child-care professional or local protective resource.

takeaway.question: What is a child-centered response to an urgent safety concern?
options: Wait for adults to present a united front.
Address immediate safety and seek appropriate help.
Ask the child to decide which caregiver is right.
takeaway.explanation: A shared approach must not override immediate safety or silence concerns.

activities.title: Reducing the strain of family logistics
activities.summary: Build a short planning loop without making one person the default manager.

cards.heading: Externalize recurring work
cards.body: A calendar, paper list or other accessible method can hold appointments, supplies, care coverage and deadlines. Use a method each person can access safely rather than assuming a particular app feature.

cards.heading: Plan for exceptions
cards.body: For each important task, identify a primary person and a willing backup. Ask what happens when a shift changes, someone is sick or transport falls through; backup should not always be the same person.

cards.heading: Set a stop time
cards.body: A short weekly review can cover what is due, who owns each item, what is overloaded and what can be dropped. Leave charged issues for a separate, consensual discussion.

cards.heading: Review the whole load
cards.body: At week’s end, check completion as well as interruption, reminders, rest and fairness. Change a plan if it relies on someone doing extra invisible coordination.

takeaway.question: Which review question checks the invisible load?
options: Who had to remember, follow up and handle exceptions?
Who looked busiest for five minutes?
Did we avoid changing the plan?
takeaway.explanation: Planning, reminders and exception handling count alongside visible completion.

activities.title: Household task audit
activities.summary: Map recurring tasks across noticing, planning, doing and checking.
activities.intro: Work alone first. Choose any household tasks relevant to you; children are not required. Use broad descriptions and skip sensitive details.

steps.prompt: List three recurring tasks, such as meals, medication pickup, bills or laundry.
For each, note who notices the need, plans, does the work and checks or follows up. Include reminders and interruptions.
What time, access, health, paid work, caregiving or other constraints shape each person’s capacity?
Which task might be clarified, simplified, shared or reassigned with agreement?

activities.outro: This is your view, not a verdict. If safe and mutually wanted, compare observations without treating disagreement as proof of bad intent.

activities.title: Our rebalance plan
activities.summary: Draft a small, revisable change in ownership and backup.
activities.intro: Draft your own proposal. A change needs the willing agreement of the people expected to do it.

steps.prompt: Choose one recurring task and write what completion includes.
Who could notice, plan, do and follow up? What information or resources would they need?
What is a realistic backup for illness, access barriers or an unusually busy week?
Suggest a start and review date, plus what would signal the plan needs adjustment.
What could be reduced so neither person simply absorbs more work?

activities.outro: If both freely agree, try the plan and revise it; otherwise seek practical support or make an individual plan.

activities.title: Parenting values comparison

activities.intro: Use only if relevant to children in your care. Reflect separately; avoid identifying details. A child’s safety comes first.

steps.prompt: Choose a routine such as leaving for school or bedtime; describe what happens without labeling the child.
Which value matters most to you in this moment?
What response could express that value while meeting the child’s needs and developmental stage?
What observation would help you tell whether the approach is helping, and when might you review it?

activities.outro: If a child is in danger, address safety immediately and seek appropriate local help rather than waiting for a comparison.

items.text: I notice qualities in my partner that I value.
It is difficult to think of a recent interaction that felt kind or respectful.

Our interactions leave little room for learning about each other.

bands.label: A place to begin

bands.label: Some room for care

bands.label: Friendship feels strained

activities.title: Making room for positive moments
activities.summary: Notice small moments of kindness without counting them against harm.

cards.heading: Pay attention, not points
cards.body: When life is crowded with logistics or tension, small pleasant interactions can go unnoticed. A shared joke or a helpful gesture may be worth noticing, but there is no magic ratio of positive to negative moments that proves a relationship is healthy.

cards.heading: Be specific
cards.body: “You made sure I had time to finish my call” describes a real action more clearly than a general demand to be positive. If the gesture mattered to you, you can say so. You never need to invent appreciation or soften a serious concern.

cards.heading: Leave room for the hard parts
cards.body: A pleasant evening does not cancel a broken agreement, erase injury, or make someone safe. Enjoyment and accountability can both matter. If fear, coercion or violence is present, do not use positive rituals to manage it; seek specialist individual support.

cards.heading: Try noticing once
cards.body: At the end of a day, recall one moment that was neutral, kind, or pleasant, if there was one. What made it possible? If nothing comes to mind, record that honestly and consider what you need rather than forcing a positive answer.

takeaway.question: How should a positive moment be understood?
options: As evidence that harm no longer matters
As one moment worth noticing, not a substitute for accountability
As a point that cancels one negative interaction
takeaway.explanation: Positive moments can be meaningful without offsetting harm.

activities.title: Fondness and admiration as a buffer
activities.summary: Practice grounded appreciation while making space for mixed feelings.

cards.heading: Remember a real quality
cards.body: Fondness can mean noticing someone’s humor, steadiness, creativity, or care. Choose a specific quality you genuinely value rather than a compliment you feel you should give. Mixed feelings are allowed, and there may be times you cannot identify one.

cards.heading: Connect quality and action
cards.body: “I value your patience when you helped our neighbor carry boxes” links a quality to something observable. It is more informative than “You are perfect.” If you choose to say it, do so without expecting praise, affection, or agreement in return.

cards.heading: Present-tense curiosity matters
cards.body: A person changes. What you admired early on may still fit, may look different now, or may no longer be true. Ask what you genuinely notice today. Avoid using a memory to imply someone must become their old self.

cards.heading: Do not make gratitude a duty
cards.body: Appreciation is not a tool for silencing pain, persuading someone to stay, or avoiding accountability. If nothing feels authentic, you can skip it. If fear, coercion or violence is present, prioritize individual specialist support.

takeaway.question: Which appreciation is most grounded?
options: You should always be more positive
I noticed you patiently helped carry those boxes; I value your care
I must praise you even when I do not mean it
takeaway.explanation: A specific and sincere observation is an invitation, not an obligation.

activities.title: Novelty and shared adventure
activities.summary: Try a new variation sized for real-world constraints.

cards.heading: Novel does not mean expensive
cards.body: A different route around the block, a new question over tea, or listening to a song can change the texture of familiar time. Adventure can happen at home or separately; it does not require travel, mobility, money, childcare, or high energy.

cards.heading: Start with constraints
cards.body: Before choosing, each person can name time, cost, access, sensory, and energy limits. A plan that ignores those limits is less likely to be enjoyable. “Ten minutes after dinner, at home, no spending” is a useful design brief.

cards.heading: Choose together, without a sales pitch
cards.body: Each person can suggest an option and decline the other’s. Look for something both genuinely want, or decide not to make a plan. No one needs to disclose a reason or agree to a compromise that feels uncomfortable.

cards.heading: Review without grading
cards.body: Afterward, ask “What was pleasant or awkward? What would we change?” An activity that fell flat is information, not a failed relationship test. Modify it, choose something else, or stop.

takeaway.question: What makes a plan accessible and low-pressure?
options: Choosing the most exciting idea regardless of constraints
Starting with both people’s time, energy, access and budget
Treating a declined idea as a rejection
takeaway.explanation: A good plan fits actual constraints and remains optional.

activities.title: Playfulness without pressure
activities.summary: Invite lightness that does not require laughter or make someone the joke.

cards.heading: Play can be quiet
cards.body: Playfulness might look like making up a silly name for a recipe, trying a new card game, or exchanging an absurd question. It need not look extroverted, competitive, physical, or sexual. Some people prefer not to play, and that is fine.

cards.heading: Consent includes humor
cards.body: A joke at someone’s expense is not playful for them if it stings. Ask whether teasing is welcome, stop if it is not, and do not demand that someone laugh. If humor is used to avoid a concern, return to the concern separately when appropriate.

cards.heading: Offer an exit
cards.body: Try an invitation with no penalty: “Want to answer one silly question, or would you rather rest?” A no is useful information. Avoid hidden tests such as “If you loved me, you would play.”

cards.heading: Keep the experiment small
cards.body: If both want to, try one five-minute activity and check whether it felt comfortable. A quiet evening, taking separate time, or discontinuing the experiment may be a better choice than pushing for fun. Play is not treatment or proof that harm is resolved.

takeaway.question: What makes a playful invitation respectful?
options: Insisting they laugh at your joke
Inviting them and accepting no without consequences
Using a joke to avoid discussing an important concern
takeaway.explanation: Playfulness works best as a choice, not a test or a way to minimize harm.

activities.title: What I first valued
activities.summary: Remember an early quality and notice whether it still fits today.
activities.intro: This is an individual reflection. You may have mixed memories or skip the activity entirely; remembering a positive moment does not require ignoring harm.

steps.prompt: Recall an early moment you genuinely enjoyed, if one comes to mind.
steps.help: Where were you and what happened? No idealized story is required.

steps.prompt: What action or quality did you value in that moment?
steps.help: Describe what you observed rather than making a broad claim.

steps.prompt: Does that quality show up differently now, or no longer fit?

steps.prompt: If you wanted to express an observation, what could you honestly say without expecting anything back?
What do you need in the present that a pleasant memory cannot resolve?

activities.summary: Build a few specific observations you genuinely believe.
activities.intro: Write only what feels authentic. This is not a scorecard or a reason to overlook harm.

steps.prompt: List up to three actions you noticed recently that you genuinely valued.

steps.prompt: Choose one action. What quality, if any, does it suggest to you?
Write a short observation and its impact on you.

steps.prompt: Does the sentence sound true and free of a hidden request? Revise or discard it.
Would you like to say it, save it for yourself, or not use it?
steps.help: A kind statement never buys agreement, affection, or forgiveness.

activities.outro: One sincere observation is enough; none is also an honest answer.

steps.prompt: What time, money, access, sensory, or energy limits matter right now?
Select one idea and make it smaller or easier.
steps.help: For example, replace a day trip with ten minutes looking at photos of a place.

steps.prompt: What is an equally valid no-cost, low-energy alternative or a way to take time alone?
If you want to invite someone, how can you make declining easy and accept their answer?

activities.outro: A list is a collection of possibilities, not a set of promises or a test of enthusiasm.

Write an invitation with an easy no and a way to reschedule only if both want to.

activities.summary: One optional, flexible shared activity per week, sized to real life.

days.task: Week 1: If both want to, pick a 10-minute, no-spend option that fits energy and access. Decide together, or choose not to plan.
Week 2: Offer one small variation, such as a different question over a drink. Either person may decline or suggest a lower-effort alternative.
Week 3: Choose an activity that accommodates the tighter time, energy, access, or budget limit; cancel if either person prefers.
Week 4: If both wish, repeat or change a favorite idea. Ask what felt good or awkward and whether to continue; no commitment is required.

activities.title: Trust Inventory
activities.summary: Reflect on reliability, honesty, emotional safety, information, and support.
activities.intro: Think about the past month and answer from your own experience. This original, unvalidated reflection is not a diagnosis, a test of whether someone is trustworthy, or a safety screen. Higher scores indicate more concern about the areas asked. A low overall score cannot establish safety. Skip or stop if you wish. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support instead of couples activities.

subscales.label: Reliability concerns
subscales.description: Whether commitments are kept or renegotiated.

subscales.label: Honesty concerns
subscales.description: Whether important information is truthful and corrected.

subscales.label: Room to express concerns
subscales.description: Whether concerns can be raised without dismissal.

subscales.label: Clarity about shared matters
subscales.description: Whether information needed for shared decisions is available.

subscales.label: Support when needed
subscales.description: Whether support requests are heard and answered clearly.

items.text: A commitment that mattered to me was not kept or renegotiated.
When a plan cannot be kept, I receive an honest update in time to make another plan.
I have discovered that something important to a shared decision was misrepresented.
When an inaccurate statement is noticed, it is corrected.
I hesitate to raise a concern because I expect it to be dismissed.
When I express hurt, there is room to hear it without demanding that I get over it.
I lack information I need to make an informed shared decision.
We can discuss what information is relevant to a shared plan while respecting individual boundaries.
When I ask for help, I am left uncertain whether it will happen.
A request for help receives a clear yes, no, or alternative.

bands.label: Fewer concerns noticed
bands.narrative: Your answers suggest fewer concerns in the areas asked. This does not prove trustworthiness or safety and does not erase a particular hurt. Choose a reflection that matters to you.

bands.label: Some concerns noticed
bands.narrative: Some aspects of trust may need attention. Look at the specific areas rather than treating the score as a verdict. You decide whether any conversation is wanted and safe.

bands.label: More concerns noticed
bands.narrative: Trust may feel strained in several areas. Individual support or, where appropriate and freely chosen, relationship support may help you consider options. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support, not couples activities.

activities.title: How trust is built in small moments
activities.summary: Make modest commitments and communicate clearly when circumstances change.

cards.heading: A clear promise can be observed
cards.body: “I will call the plumber by Thursday afternoon” is easier to evaluate than “I will be more dependable.” Only promise what you can reasonably do. A clear no is preferable to a reluctant yes.

cards.heading: Acknowledge changes early
cards.body: If a plan becomes impossible, give an honest update as soon as practical: “I cannot call today; would Friday work, or would you rather make another plan?” The other person can decline the revision.

cards.heading: Look at patterns, not a single signal
cards.body: One kept promise may be useful information; it does not erase earlier harm or prove future trustworthiness. The person affected decides what the evidence means to them.

cards.heading: Trust is not an obligation
cards.body: Someone can notice improvement and still want distance, boundaries, or separation. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support instead of rebuilding trust together.

takeaway.question: What makes a commitment easier to evaluate?
options: An assurance that nothing will ever go wrong.
takeaway.explanation: Specific actions make it possible to see what happened, without guaranteeing an outcome.

activities.title: Betrayal comes in many forms
activities.summary: Name the action and impact without deciding what another person must forgive.

cards.heading: Begin with the concrete event
cards.body: Trust can be strained by a broken commitment, a lie about a shared expense, or not showing up after offering help. What matters is the action, its context, and its impact—not a competition over who has suffered more.

cards.heading: Separate privacy from deception
cards.body: People can have personal boundaries and private information. A missed disclosure may matter when it affects a shared decision, but privacy alone is not proof of betrayal or permission to monitor someone.

cards.heading: Name impacts without forcing a narrative
cards.body: An affected person might feel anger, uncertainty, or no immediate reaction. They choose what to share. The person who acted can listen without demanding a timeline for recovery.

cards.heading: Consider what kind of support fits
cards.body: This module addresses everyday trust concerns, not a full response to infidelity, coercion, or violence. For fear or abuse, seek individual safety and specialized support instead of couples activities.

takeaway.question: Which statement respects both trust and individual boundaries?
options: “Personal privacy alone is not proof of deception.”
“To prove trust, everyone must share passwords.”
takeaway.explanation: A shared decision may require relevant information; it does not erase individual boundaries.

activities.title: What real accountability looks like
activities.summary: Acknowledge an action and impact without excuses, then offer a specific repair.

cards.heading: Identify what you did
cards.body: Say what happened in concrete terms: “I said I had paid the bill when I had not.” Avoid vague phrases like “mistakes were made” or “sorry you felt that way.”

cards.heading: Hear the impact
cards.body: If the affected person wants to speak, listen without correcting their feelings. “You had to spend time fixing the late fee, and it left you uncertain about the budget.” Check whether you understood.

cards.heading: Own the choice; offer, do not demand
cards.body: “I chose not to tell you. That was my responsibility. I will pay the fee and tell you when the payment is made, if that is useful.” Do not blame the other person or ask for immediate reassurance.

cards.heading: Follow through and allow a no
cards.body: Make a feasible plan, act on it, and correct any new mistake. The affected person can refuse a conversation or repair, take space, or leave. An apology is not a transaction for renewed trust.

takeaway.question: Which apology includes ownership without pressure?
options: “I hid the missed payment; I am responsible and will pay the fee.”
“I am sorry, but you made it hard to tell you.”
“I apologized, so you must trust me.”
takeaway.explanation: It names the action and a repair without placing responsibility on the affected person.

activities.title: Consistency over grand gestures
activities.summary: Use a limited, observable plan instead of a dramatic promise.

cards.heading: Make the promise fit your control
cards.body: “I will submit the payment by Friday” is within your control; “you will feel safe again by Friday” is not. Agree only to actions you can actually take.

cards.heading: Set a check, not a deadline for trust
cards.body: Choose a short review period and how to observe the action, such as a receipt for a shared bill. Avoid demanding passwords, device access, location tracking, or unlimited disclosure.

cards.heading: When a plan fails
cards.body: Acknowledge the miss promptly without hiding it: “I missed Friday. I will submit it today; would another arrangement work better?” The other person may choose a different plan or boundary.

cards.heading: Let the affected person decide
cards.body: Consistency can provide information, not an entitlement to closeness. Someone may still choose distance, a different arrangement, or separation. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support.

takeaway.question: What can a person reasonably promise?
options: That a partner will trust them by a deadline.
A specific action they control, with an honest update if it changes.
That they will never make any mistake.
takeaway.explanation: A commitment should describe behavior within the person’s control.

activities.title: Shame vs. guilt for the partner who broke trust
activities.summary: Use discomfort as a prompt for ownership, not a request to be reassured.

cards.heading: Distinguish action from identity
cards.body: “I did something harmful” focuses on an action and possible repair. “I am irredeemable” can consume the conversation without helping the affected person. Feelings are real, but they do not themselves repair harm.

cards.heading: Avoid making the hurt person manage your distress
cards.body: You might say “I need a moment to steady myself; I will seek support separately.” Do not demand that the affected person comfort you or tell you that you are a good person.

cards.heading: Return to the actionable part
cards.body: Write what you did, what the impact was if known, and what action you can take or offer. If the other person declines contact, respect that decision and work on your behavior independently.

cards.heading: Own only your own conduct
cards.body: Shame is not an excuse or a reason to accept responsibility for someone else’s coercion or violence. Individual support can help you sort responsibility and boundaries without forcing a joint process.

takeaway.question: What is a constructive response to shame after causing harm?
options: Ask the hurt person to reassure you immediately.
Seek support separately and focus on the action you can own.
takeaway.explanation: Separately managing distress leaves room for accountability without demanding comfort.

activities.title: Our trust timeline
activities.summary: Map significant moments and your response without having to share the record.
activities.intro: Work alone on a manageable example. Skip details or steps and stop whenever you wish; sharing is optional. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support instead of couples activities.

steps.prompt: Choose a manageable period. You can omit details or stop; do not record sensitive information if doing so could put you at risk.
List up to three events that affected your trust, using brief factual descriptions and approximate dates.
Choose one event. What changed for you in practical terms, feelings, or decisions? Separate what you observed from what you inferred.
What happened afterward: an acknowledgement, a repair, a repeated behavior, or no response? What remains uncertain?
What boundary, support, or next step do you want now? Sharing the timeline or seeking reconciliation is optional.

activities.outro: Keep, revise, or discard your reflection. A draft is not an agreement and does not require contact or reconciliation.

activities.title: Promises I can actually keep
activities.summary: Draft a specific commitment within your control and a plan for change.
activities.intro: Work alone on a manageable example. Skip details or steps and stop whenever you wish; sharing is optional. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support instead of couples activities.

steps.prompt: Choose a small action relevant to a shared plan or your own reliability. Avoid promising someone else’s feelings or response.
Write what you will do and by when: “I will ___ by ___.” Check that it is within your control and capacity.
What might get in the way? What will you do if that happens, and how will you communicate a change if appropriate?
How could the action be observed without surveillance or sharing passwords, locations, or private messages? A receipt for a shared expense is one possible example.
Offer the commitment only if welcome. The other person may decline it or choose a different boundary. Do not use the promise to demand trust or contact.

activities.outro: Keep, revise, or discard your reflection. A draft is not an agreement and does not require contact or reconciliation.

activities.title: Transparency agreements
activities.summary: Plan a narrow exchange of relevant information without trading away privacy or autonomy.
activities.intro: Work alone on a manageable example. Skip details or steps and stop whenever you wish; sharing is optional. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support instead of couples activities.

steps.prompt: Identify one shared decision for which information is needed, such as a joint bill. What specific information is relevant?
What information is not needed? Exclude passwords, unrestricted device access, location monitoring, and private messages as default requirements.
Draft a bounded proposal: who would share which information, how often, for how long, and for what purpose? Both people must be free to say no.
If either declines, what alternative could protect each person’s boundary while addressing the shared decision? It is acceptable to have no agreement.
Only if both voluntarily agree and it is safe, choose when to review or end the arrangement. Stop if it becomes monitoring, pressure, or control; seek individual specialized support if needed.

activities.outro: Keep, revise, or discard your reflection. A draft is not an agreement and does not require contact or reconciliation.

activities.title: Weekly reliability log
activities.summary: Record a few commitments and what happened, including honest changes.
activities.intro: Work alone on a manageable example. Skip details or steps and stop whenever you wish; sharing is optional. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support instead of couples activities.

steps.prompt: List up to three specific commitments you chose to make this week, with a due time. Do not track someone without their consent.
For each, note “kept,” “changed with an update,” “missed,” or “not yet due.” Record facts rather than judgments about character.
If you missed a commitment, what was the impact if known? What corrective action or honest update can you offer without demanding a response?
Which commitment should be smaller, changed, or discontinued next week? What capacity do you actually have?
Review this record for your own choices. Another person is not obliged to inspect it, provide reassurance, or renew trust.

activities.title: Where trust lives for me
activities.summary: Explore your own evidence, boundaries, and choices without a forced outcome.
activities.intro: Choose what is safe to record, skip any prompt, and stop whenever you wish. You do not have to share. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support.
prompts: What specific event or pattern affected my trust? What did I observe, and what remains uncertain?
What practical impact did it have on me? What feelings or needs do I notice without judging them?
What actions, if any, would be useful evidence of change? Which decisions or feelings remain mine to make?
What boundaries about contact, information, time, or support do I want to maintain?
What options—including space, individual support, or ending the relationship—do I want to consider? I do not have to decide today.

activities.title: 14 days of small kept promises
activities.summary: Practice realistic commitments and honest updates without demanding trust.
activities.intro: This is a solo practice. Choose commitments within your control, and skip or stop whenever needed. No one owes you contact, forgiveness, or reconciliation. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, prioritize individual safety and specialized support, not couples activities.

days.task: Choose one small action you control and set a realistic time for it.
Carry out or honestly revise the action; notice what helped or got in the way.
Choose a commitment small enough to fit your actual capacity today.
If plans change, practice an early, honest update where appropriate.
Review a missed commitment without excuses; identify one corrective action you can take.
If an offer of help is welcome, make it specific and accept a no.
Review your week: which promise was feasible, and what should change?
Choose one task with a clear finish, not a promise about someone else’s feelings.
Complete the task or name the obstacle and revise your plan honestly.
If a shared plan is affected, provide the relevant update without requiring a response.
Practice saying a clear, respectful no to a commitment you cannot keep.
Take one practical corrective step on a past miss, without demanding forgiveness.
Choose a small action that respects another person’s stated boundaries.
Review the two weeks and decide what you will continue, change, or stop. Another person decides what the evidence means to them.

activities.title: Shared Meaning
activities.summary: Notice where values, daily rituals, roles, and future hopes need attention.
activities.intro: Think about the past month and the kind of relationship or independent future you want. Skip anything that does not fit. This original educational reflection is not a validated measure, diagnosis, or decision about whether to stay. A score cannot establish safety. If fear, coercion, or violence is present, seek specialist individual support rather than couples activities.

bands.narrative: Your answers suggest fewer areas of strain among the questions answered. Values and plans can still change; this result does not establish safety or predict your future.

bands.label: Some questions to explore

activities.title: Making room for a shared why
activities.summary: Explore values in common without requiring identical priorities.

cards.heading: Meaning is not a slogan
cards.body: Values are directions that help you choose, such as fairness, curiosity, faith, stability, generosity, or independence. Two people may value the same word but mean different things by it. A useful shared “why” begins with asking what the word looks like in daily life.

cards.heading: Start with your own meaning
cards.body: Choose two values and complete: “I know this matters when I make room for…” For example, stability might mean predictable bills to one person and a familiar home to another. Be specific before deciding whether your meanings overlap.

cards.heading: Difference is information
cards.body: Partners do not need identical values or a single life plan. If freedom and stability pull in different directions, name the concrete tension rather than asking either person to surrender a core need. Some differences may remain unresolved or affect decisions about the relationship.

cards.heading: Try a small expression
cards.body: If it feels right, choose an action under your control that expresses one value this week. If both people freely want a conversation and feel safe, ask what their chosen value means to them. Do not use shared language to excuse harm or pressure someone to stay.

takeaway.question: What makes a values conversation useful?
options: Assuming the same word means the same thing
Asking what each person means and allowing differences
Demanding a single shared answer immediately
takeaway.explanation: A shared direction, if wanted, starts with understanding individual meanings.

activities.title: Rituals of connection
activities.summary: Design repeatable moments that can change or end.

cards.heading: A ritual is a repeated choice
cards.body: A ritual is an ordinary action with a meaning you attach to it: a quiet tea, a greeting, a weekly walk, or a solo pause before bed. It need not involve touch, cost money, or include another person. Repetition is useful only while it still fits.

cards.heading: Make it small enough to survive real life
cards.body: Name a cue, action, and flexible length: “After I put the kettle on, I take two quiet breaths.” Consider access, disability, caregiving, work, and energy. A version that takes one minute may be more sustainable than an idealized hour.

cards.heading: Invite rather than assign
cards.body: For a shared ritual, ask whether the other person wants it and what would make it comfortable. Either person can say no, skip a day, or change their mind. An invitation is not evidence that a partner has agreed.

cards.heading: Review the meaning
cards.body: After a week, ask whether the ritual actually supported the purpose you chose. If a routine creates pressure or resentment, reduce it, change it, or stop. A missed day is not a relationship verdict.

takeaway.question: What belongs in a flexible ritual?
options: A cue, a small action, and permission to change or skip
A rule that neither person may ever miss it
An activity the other person has not agreed to
takeaway.explanation: A ritual can be useful and still remain voluntary and adaptable.

activities.title: What our roles mean to each of us
activities.summary: Translate labels into responsibilities, choice, and support.

cards.heading: A title can hide different expectations
cards.body: Words such as partner, parent, provider, caregiver, or homemaker carry cultural and personal meanings. None of these roles is required for a relationship. Ask what a label means to you rather than assuming another person shares your definition.

cards.heading: Look at the invisible parts
cards.body: A responsibility often includes noticing, planning, arranging, doing, and following up. “Handle dinner” may include checking supplies, accommodating needs, shopping, cooking, and cleaning. Name the pieces before judging whether an arrangement is workable.

cards.heading: Check authority and capacity
cards.body: Who can make decisions? Who has time, resources, access, or energy? Is anyone expected to take on work without freely agreeing? A fair arrangement accounts for paid work, care, health, and personal time; equal numbers of tasks are not necessarily equal effort.

cards.heading: Make a reversible experiment
cards.body: If both freely want to and feel safe, choose one specific task, person, scope, and review date. Either person can say a role or arrangement does not work. Safety, bodily autonomy, and access to basic resources are not bargaining chips.

takeaway.question: What helps make a role discussion concrete?
options: Assuming a title has one universal meaning
Naming the planning, doing, and follow-up a task involves
Counting tasks without considering time or capacity
takeaway.explanation: Specific responsibilities and real constraints reveal more than labels.

activities.title: Growing apart and growing together
activities.summary: Make space for change without treating a shared future as mandatory.

cards.heading: People and circumstances change
cards.body: Career hopes, health, identity, caregiving, finances, beliefs, or interests may shift. Change does not automatically mean a relationship is failing, and sameness is not the only way to remain connected. It is also possible to decide that a relationship no longer fits.

cards.heading: Ask about directions, not predictions
cards.body: A five-year picture is a possibility, not a forecast or promise. Ask what you want more or less of and what feels uncertain. A person may hope for stability while another wants change; neither must make their hope disappear to keep the conversation comfortable.

cards.heading: Separate the negotiable from the essential
cards.body: For each hope, name one flexible detail and one important need. “I want meaningful work” might allow several locations; “I need control over my own money” is not a bargaining chip. If a difference involves safety or coercion, seek specialist individual support.

cards.heading: Take a small step without deciding everything
cards.body: Try gathering information, protecting time for an interest, or revisiting a question in a month. If both freely want to talk, exchange perspectives without requiring a joint plan. Either person can pause, revise, or choose a different path.

takeaway.question: How should a five-year vision be treated?
options: As one possible direction that can be revised
As proof that both people must stay together
takeaway.explanation: A vision is a tool for reflection, not a commitment or prediction.

steps.prompt: Imagine an ordinary day about five years from now. What would you like more or less of?

steps.prompt: Which value is visible in that imagined day? What does it look like in practice?
What feels uncertain or outside your control?

steps.prompt: Which parts feel important to your autonomy or wellbeing, and which details could change?
What is one information-gathering or low-cost step you could take in the next month?
When might you revisit the picture, knowing you may choose a different path?

activities.outro: Your vision belongs to you and is allowed to change.

days.task: Name a purpose you care about, such as rest, curiosity, or connection.

Notice whether the action supports your purpose; change it if it does not.

Remove one unnecessary step or cost.
Choose a fallback for busy or low-energy days, including taking a day off.

Notice whose needs the routine serves and whether anyone feels pressure; change or stop if needed.
Try the current version only if it still feels useful and wanted.
